gloss: fearing too much and too readily, and having too little confidence, in the face of danger
gloss_modern: This means fearing danger too much and too readily, and lacking the confidence to face it.
reasoning: Aristotle's deficiency in facing danger is fearing too much and too readily, with too little confidence. Today this is the person who is easily frightened and shrinks from risks that should be faced.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: feeling fear and confidence in the right measure when facing danger, and standing firm for a worthy end
gloss_modern: This means facing danger with fear and confidence in due measure, and standing firm for a worthy cause.
reasoning: The mean is the person who feels fear and confidence in due measure and stands firm for a worthy end. Today we call this person brave.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: having too much confidence: rushing at danger with no proper sense of the risk
gloss_modern: This means charging into danger with too much confidence and no real grasp of the risk involved.
reasoning: The excess is too much confidence, rushing at danger without a proper sense of the risk. Today this is the reckless person who charges ahead heedlessly.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: taking too little pleasure in food, drink and sex; a type Aristotle says is rarely met
gloss_modern: This means taking too little enjoyment in food, drink and sex, and seeming dull to bodily delights.
reasoning: This is taking too little pleasure in food, drink and sex, a rare type for Aristotle. Today it is the person who is cold and indifferent to bodily delights; the old word 'insensibility' now means numbness, so a plain phrase is used.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: enjoying the pleasures of the body in the right measure, at the right times, without being ruled by them
gloss_modern: This means enjoying bodily pleasures in due measure and at fitting times, never being ruled by them.
reasoning: The mean is enjoying bodily pleasures in due measure and at fitting times without being ruled by them. Today this is the temperate, self-controlled person.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: pursuing the pleasures of food, drink and sex to excess and being pained when they are missing
gloss_modern: This means chasing food, drink and sex to excess, and being distressed when they are unavailable.
reasoning: The excess is pursuing food, drink and sex to excess and suffering when they are absent. Today this is the self-indulgent, intemperate person.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: giving too little and taking too much where money is concerned
gloss_modern: This means giving too little and grasping too much where money is concerned.
reasoning: This is giving too little and grasping too much with money. Today this is the stingy, grasping person.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: giving and taking money in the right measure, to the right people, with pleasure
gloss_modern: This means giving and taking money in the right amounts, to the right people, and gladly.
reasoning: The mean is giving and taking money in the right measure, to the right people, with pleasure. Today this is the generous person.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: giving and spending money far too freely, wasting one's substance
gloss_modern: This means spending and giving money far too freely, squandering one's wealth.
reasoning: The excess is spending and giving money far too freely, wasting one's means. Today this is the wasteful, spendthrift person.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: spending too little on great public occasions, spoiling the effect to save a little
gloss_modern: This means spending too little on grand occasions and public works, spoiling the effect to save money.
reasoning: This is spending too little on great public occasions, spoiling the effect to save a little. Today this is the penny-pinching person who cheapens grand occasions.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: spending large sums fittingly and with taste on great occasions and public works
gloss_modern: This means spending large sums tastefully and fittingly on great occasions and public works.
reasoning: The mean is spending large sums fittingly and tastefully on great occasions and public works. Today this is the person who gives generously on a grand scale.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: spending lavishly on display where it is not fitting, to show off one's wealth
gloss_modern: This means spending lavishly on display where it is unfitting, just to show off one's wealth.
reasoning: The excess is lavish display where it is unfitting, done to show off wealth. Today this is the showy person who flaunts money.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: thinking oneself worthy of less than one deserves, and so not claiming one's due
gloss_modern: This means underrating oneself and failing to claim the recognition one deserves.
reasoning: This is thinking oneself worth less than one is, and so failing to claim one's due. Today this is the person who lacks self-regard and undervalues themselves.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: thinking oneself worthy of great things and being worthy of them
gloss_modern: This means rightly regarding oneself as worthy of great things, and truly being worthy of them.
reasoning: The mean is rightly thinking oneself worthy of great things and truly being worthy of them. Today this is the person of lofty, dignified self-respect.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: thinking oneself worthy of great things without being worthy of them
gloss_modern: This means thinking oneself worthy of great honours without having earned them.
reasoning: The excess is thinking oneself worthy of great things without being so. Today this is the conceited, self-important person.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: caring too little for honor, even for the honor that would be fitting
gloss_modern: This means caring too little about honour, even the honour one fittingly deserves.
reasoning: This is caring too little for honour, even the honour one fittingly deserves. Today this is the person with no drive for recognition or achievement.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: desiring honor as one should and from the right sources; a mean Aristotle says has no name
gloss_modern: This means desiring honour as one should, from worthy sources and in due measure.
reasoning: The mean is desiring honour as one should, from the right sources and in due measure. Aristotle says it has no name, so a plain phrase is used for the healthy drive for worthy recognition.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: desiring honor more than is right, and from the wrong sources
gloss_modern: This means craving honour beyond what is right, and chasing it from shallow or wrong sources.
reasoning: The excess is desiring honour beyond what is right and from wrong sources. Today this is the vain, glory-seeking person.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: not getting angry even when anger is called for, and putting up with insult
gloss_modern: This means never getting angry even when anger is due, and tamely enduring insults.
reasoning: This is failing to get angry even when anger is called for, and putting up with insult. Today this is the person who tamely submits to mistreatment.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: being angry at the right things, with the right people, to the right degree and for the right length of time
gloss_modern: This means getting angry at the right things, with the right people, to the right degree and length.
reasoning: The mean is getting angry at the right things, with the right people, to the right degree and for the right length of time. Today this is the calm, even-tempered person who resents what deserves resentment.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: getting angry quickly, too often and too much, at the wrong things
gloss_modern: This means flying into anger quickly and often, at trivial or wrongly chosen targets.
reasoning: Irascibility is the excess of good temper: anger that flares too quickly, too often, and at the wrong things. Today this is the hot-tempered person who is easily provoked.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: understating or disclaiming one's own merits and achievements
gloss_modern: This means understating your own merits and achievements, disclaiming credit you have actually earned.
reasoning: Mock modesty is the deficiency of truthfulness: disclaiming or understating one's own real merits. Today this is the person who falsely plays down their achievements, fishing for praise or hiding behind feigned humility.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: presenting oneself, in word and in life, as neither more nor less than one is
gloss_modern: This means representing yourself accurately in speech and conduct, neither inflating nor understating what you are.
reasoning: Truthfulness is the mean of presenting oneself accurately in word and deed. The truthful person is honest about who they are, claiming neither more nor less than is so.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: claiming merits and achievements one does not have, or more of them than one has
gloss_modern: This means claiming achievements you do not have, or inflating the ones you do have.
reasoning: Boastfulness is the excess of truthfulness: claiming merits one lacks or exaggerating those one has. Today this is the boastful person who brags.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: making no jokes and taking offense at those who do
gloss_modern: This means refusing to joke and bristling at others' banter, as if their wit were aimed at you.
reasoning: Boorishness is the deficiency of ready wit: making no jokes and resenting those who do. Today this is the humorless, stiff person who takes teasing as an insult.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: joking tastefully and in the right measure in relaxed company
gloss_modern: This means joking well, with taste and proportion, and enjoying lighthearted company without causing hurt.
reasoning: Ready wit is the mean of tasteful, well-measured joking in relaxed company. The witty person is quick with amusing remarks that suit the moment and do not hurt.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: trying to raise a laugh at any cost, with no regard for decency or for the feelings of the target
gloss_modern: This means playing the fool for laughs at any cost, careless of decency and of whom the joke wounds.
reasoning: Buffoonery is the excess of ready wit: clowning for laughs at any cost, with no regard for decency or for whoever is the butt of the joke. Today this is the buffoon or clown.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: opposing everything and caring nothing for the pain one causes in company
gloss_modern: This means opposing whatever others say and not minding how much discomfort it causes in company.
reasoning: Quarrelsomeness is the deficiency of friendliness: contradicting everyone and not caring how much pain one causes in company. Today this is the argumentative, combative person.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: being pleasant in company as one should, approving and objecting in the right measure
gloss_modern: This means being pleasant company, agreeing and objecting in measure, without flattering or quarreling.
reasoning: Friendliness is the mean of being pleasant in company, agreeing and objecting in the right measure. The friendly person is warm and easy to be with without flattering or fighting.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: praising everything and never opposing, so as to give no pain; done for gain it is flattery
gloss_modern: This means praising everything and never objecting, so as to spare pain, and flattering for personal gain.
reasoning: Obsequiousness is the excess of friendliness: praising everything and never objecting to spare others pain, and when done for gain it is flattery. Today this is the fawning, servile flatterer.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: feeling no shame at all, even at disgraceful acts
gloss_modern: This means feeling no shame whatsoever, even when one commits acts that are disgraceful.
reasoning: Shamelessness is the deficiency of modesty: feeling no shame at all, even at disgraceful acts. Today this is the brazen person who is unembarrassed by disgrace.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: feeling shame in the right measure at what is disgraceful
gloss_modern: This means feeling shame in due measure at disgraceful conduct, and not at things that are innocent.
reasoning: Modesty is the mean of feeling shame in due measure at what is disgraceful. The modest person blushes at real disgrace and is not troubled by innocent matters.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: being ashamed of everything, too easily and too much
gloss_modern: This means blushing and feeling ashamed at almost everything, far too readily and too intensely.
reasoning: Bashfulness is the excess of modesty: being ashamed of everything too easily and too much. Today this is the person who is easily embarrassed and shy.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: falling so short of being pained at others' undeserved good fortune that one rejoices at their ill fortune
gloss_modern: This means taking pleasure in others' bad luck and feeling no pain when undeserved good luck comes their way.
reasoning: Spite is the deficiency of righteous indignation: feeling too little pain at others' undeserved good fortune that one rejoices in their misfortune. Today this is the malicious, spiteful person.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: being pained at good fortune that is undeserved
gloss_modern: This means feeling pained when good fortune reaches people who do not deserve it, and not when they do.
reasoning: Righteous indignation is the mean of being pained at undeserved good fortune. The person with it resents injustice in others' success while accepting what is deserved.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: being pained at all good fortune of others, deserved or not
gloss_modern: This means being pained by every good thing that happens to others, whether they deserve it or not.
reasoning: Envy is the excess of righteous indignation: being pained by every good fortune of others, deserved or not. Today this is the envious person who resents others' success.
source: Nicomachean Ethics II.7 (Ross); the fuller accounts in III.6-IV.9

gloss: living with no regard for anyone else, taking no account of what others want
gloss_modern: This means ignoring what others want and living as you please, with no account taken of anyone else.
reasoning: Self-will is the deficiency of dignity: living with no regard for others and ignoring what they want. Today this is the headstrong, inconsiderate person who does as they please.
source: Eudemian Ethics II.3 (Rackham); the fuller account in III.7

gloss: keeping a proper measure of regard for others, neither ignoring them nor living only to please them
gloss_modern: This means giving others their due regard, neither ignoring them nor living only to please them.
reasoning: Dignity is the mean of keeping a proper measure of regard for others, neither ignoring nor serving them. The dignified person carries self-respect while respecting others.
source: Eudemian Ethics II.3 (Rackham); the fuller account in III.7

gloss: adjusting everything to what others want, living to please them
gloss_modern: This means bending everything to others' wishes and living only to please them, with no will of one's own.
reasoning: Subservience is the excess of dignity: adjusting everything to others' wishes and living only to please them. Today this is the servile, obsequious person who has no will of their own.
source: Eudemian Ethics II.3 (Rackham); the fuller account in III.7

gloss: lacking the shrewdness to see how to reach one's ends, and so being easily taken in
gloss_modern: This means lacking the shrewdness to see how to reach one's goals, so that others easily deceive one.
reasoning: Simpleness is the deficiency of practical wisdom: lacking the shrewdness to see how to reach one's ends, so one is easily taken in. Today this is the trusting, gullible person who is easily deceived.
source: Eudemian Ethics II.3 (Rackham); the fuller account in III.7

gloss: deliberating well about what is good for a human life and how to achieve it
gloss_modern: This means judging well what is good for a whole human life and how to reach it.
reasoning: Practical wisdom is the mean between simpleness and rascality: the capacity to deliberate well about what is good for a whole human life and how to achieve it. A person who has it is sound in judgment about how to live and act, which today we call sagacity.
source: Eudemian Ethics II.3 (Rackham); the fuller account in III.7

gloss: being clever at reaching any end at all, good or bad; cunning without scruple
gloss_modern: This means using cleverness to reach any goal at all, good or bad, with no moral restraint.
reasoning: Rascality is the excess of practical wisdom: skill at reaching any end, good or bad, without moral restraint. Today this is a person who is clever and calculating but has no scruples about how they get what they want.
source: Eudemian Ethics II.3 (Rackham); the fuller account in III.7

gloss: hiding one's real thoughts and plans behind friendly words, pretending to know or intend nothing
gloss_modern: This means hiding one's real aims behind friendly words while feigning ignorance of any plan.
reasoning: Theophrastus' dissembler hides his real thoughts and plans behind friendly words and pretends to know or intend nothing. Today this is a duplicitous person whose manner conceals what they are really up to.
source: Theophrastus, Characters 1 (Jebb 1870: "The Dissembler")

gloss: praising and fawning on someone in order to profit by it
gloss_modern: This means praising and fawning over someone to gain something from them, not from honest admiration.
reasoning: The flatterer praises and fawns on someone in order to profit by it, not from genuine admiration. Today this is a sycophant who ingratiates themselves for gain.
source: Theophrastus, Characters 2 (Jebb 1870: "The Flatterer")

gloss: pouring out long, rambling talk on trivial matters to anyone who cannot escape
gloss_modern: This means rambling on at length about trivia to anyone unable to escape the conversation.
reasoning: The garrulous man pours out long, rambling talk on trivial matters to anyone who cannot get away. Today this is a long-winded talker who bores captive listeners.
source: Theophrastus, Characters 3 (Jebb 1870: "The Garrulous Man")

gloss: ignorance of social manners: coarse, uncouth and loud in company
gloss_modern: This means lacking social polish, being coarse, loud and rude in company.
reasoning: The boor is ignorant of social manners and is coarse, uncouth and loud in company. Today this is a person who lacks polish and offends people through crude behavior.
source: Theophrastus, Characters 4 (Jebb 1870: "The Boor")

gloss: trying to please everyone and to give no offense, agreeing with all sides
gloss_modern: This means eagerly pleasing everyone, agreeing with every side, and avoiding any offense.
reasoning: The complaisant man tries to please everyone and give no offense, agreeing with all sides. Today this is an obsequious person whose eagerness to please has become servile and spineless.
source: Theophrastus, Characters 5 (Jebb 1870: "The Complaisant Man")

gloss: loss of all sense of shame or scruple in word and deed, ready to do anything disreputable
gloss_modern: This means feeling no shame in word or deed and readily doing anything disreputable.
reasoning: Theophrastus' reckless man has lost all sense of shame or scruple in word and deed and will do anything disreputable. Today this is a brazen person with no principles restraining them.
source: Theophrastus, Characters 6 (Jebb 1870: "The Reckless Man")

gloss: talking incessantly, unable to hold one's tongue, interrupting and holding forth
gloss_modern: This means talking incessantly, unable to hold one's tongue, interrupting others and holding forth.
reasoning: The loquacious man talks incessantly, cannot hold his tongue, interrupts and holds forth. Today this is someone who dominates conversation and cannot stop talking.
source: Theophrastus, Characters 7 (Jebb 1870: "The Talker")

gloss: inventing news and rumors and passing them on as fact
gloss_modern: This means inventing news and rumors and passing them off as established fact.
reasoning: The rumor-monger invents news and rumors and passes them on as fact. Today this is a person who spreads falsehoods as if they were true, which is more than idle gossip.
source: Theophrastus, Characters 8 (Jebb 1870: "The Newsmaker")

gloss: disregarding one's reputation for the sake of petty gain, such as cheating creditors or sponging
gloss_modern: This means discarding one's good name for petty gain, such as cheating creditors or freeloading.
reasoning: The shameless man disregards his reputation for petty gain, such as cheating creditors or sponging off others. Today this is a disreputable person who will sink to small swindles and freeloading.
source: Theophrastus, Characters 9 (Jebb 1870: "The Shameless Man")

gloss: excessive economy over tiny sums, counting every coin
gloss_modern: This means guarding even trivial sums so closely that one counts every coin.
reasoning: The penurious man is excessively economical over tiny sums and counts every coin. Today this is a stingy person who grudges even trivial spending.
source: Theophrastus, Characters 10 (Jebb 1870: "The Penurious Man")

gloss: open, offensive indecency and coarse jesting in public
gloss_modern: This means openly flaunting offensive indecency and telling coarse jokes in public.
reasoning: The gross man openly commits offensive indecency and tells coarse jokes in public. Today this is a vulgar person with no sense of decorum, who flaunts crudeness.
source: Theophrastus, Characters 11 (Jebb 1870: "The Gross Man")

gloss: choosing the wrong time for everything, to the annoyance of those one deals with
gloss_modern: This means picking the wrong moment for everything, irritating the people one deals with.
reasoning: The man of poor timing chooses the wrong moment for everything, to the annoyance of those he deals with. Today this is a tactless person who lacks a sense of when to speak or act.
source: Theophrastus, Characters 12 (Jebb 1870: "The Unseasonable Man")

gloss: well-meant but overeager readiness to help, promise and interfere
gloss_modern: This means eagerly offering help, making promises and interfering where it is unwanted.
reasoning: The officious man is overeager to help, promise and interfere, though his zeal is well meant. Today this is a meddlesome person who intrudes where help is unwanted.
source: Theophrastus, Characters 13 (Jebb 1870: "The Officious Man")

gloss: slowness of mind in word and act; forgetting, missing the point
gloss_modern: This means being slow to grasp things, forgetting easily, and missing the point in word and action.
reasoning: Theophrastus' stupid man is slow of mind in word and act, forgetting things and missing the point. Today this is a slow-witted person who grasps things poorly.
source: Theophrastus, Characters 14 (Jebb 1870: "The Stupid Man")

gloss: rudeness and ungraciousness in speech, refusing courtesy
gloss_modern: This means being rude and ungracious in speech, refusing even ordinary courtesy.
reasoning: The surly man is rude and ungracious in speech and refuses ordinary courtesy. Today this is a churlish, bad-tempered person who treats others with contempt.
source: Theophrastus, Characters 15 (Jebb 1870: "The Surly Man")

gloss: cowardice toward the supernatural, fussing over omens, rites and pollution
gloss_modern: This means being frightened of the supernatural, fussing over omens, rites and ritual pollution.
reasoning: The superstitious man is cowardly toward the supernatural, fussing over omens, rites and pollution. Today this is a person governed by irrational fear of the supernatural.
source: Theophrastus, Characters 16 (Jebb 1870: "The Superstitious Man")

gloss: unreasonable fault-finding with one's lot, complaining even of favors
gloss_modern: This means finding fault with one's lot unreasonably, complaining even about favors received.
reasoning: The grumbler finds unreasonable fault with his lot and complains even about favors he receives. Today this is a querulous person who is never satisfied.
source: Theophrastus, Characters 17 (Jebb 1870: "The Grumbler")

gloss: presuming dishonesty in everyone, checking up on all
gloss_modern: This means assuming everyone is dishonest and constantly checking up on people.
reasoning: The distrustful man presumes everyone dishonest and checks up on all. Today this is a suspicious person who cannot take others at their word.
source: Theophrastus, Characters 18 (Jebb 1870: "The Distrustful Man")

gloss: neglect of one's person to the point of disgusting others
gloss_modern: This means neglecting grooming and hygiene so thoroughly that one's appearance and smell repel the people nearby.
reasoning: The Greek vice is neglect of one's person to the point of repelling others. Today this is a person who is untidy and unwashed, so that their appearance and smell put others off.
source: Theophrastus, Characters 19 (Jebb 1870: "The Offensive Man")

gloss: behavior that causes annoyance without doing harm: tactless remarks, embarrassing stories
gloss_modern: This means saying awkward, embarrassing things at the wrong moments, irritating people without meaning any real harm.
reasoning: This vice is causing annoyance without real harm, through tactless remarks and embarrassing stories. Today it describes someone who lacks social sensitivity and irritates others with boorish talk.
source: Theophrastus, Characters 20 (Jebb 1870: "The Unpleasant Man")

gloss: an ignoble desire for distinction, seeking credit and display in trifles
gloss_modern: This means angling for applause and credit through showy displays over trivial matters, keeping oneself constantly in the spotlight.
reasoning: This is an ignoble craving for distinction, pursued through show and credit for trifles. Today it describes a person who seeks attention and applause for minor achievements.
source: Theophrastus, Characters 21 (Jebb 1870: "The Man of Petty Ambition")

gloss: lack of generosity where honor or expense is concerned, avoiding any outlay
gloss_modern: This means refusing to spend or give, even when generosity or honor calls for it, and avoiding every small outlay.
reasoning: This is a lack of generosity in matters of honor or expense, avoiding any outlay. Today it is a person who is unwilling to spend money or give anything away.
source: Theophrastus, Characters 22 (Jebb 1870: "The Mean Man")

gloss: pretending to advantages, wealth or connections one does not have
gloss_modern: This means claiming wealth, influence or connections one does not have, and talking up one's standing to impress others.
reasoning: This vice is pretending to advantages, wealth or connections one lacks. Today it describes a person who brags falsely about their status and achievements.
source: Theophrastus, Characters 23 (Jebb 1870: "The Boastful Man")

gloss: contempt for everyone except oneself, refusing to give anyone their due
gloss_modern: This means looking down on everyone else and refusing to give others the respect or recognition they deserve.
reasoning: This is contempt for everyone but oneself, with a refusal to give others their due. Today it describes a person who looks down on others and feels entitled to special treatment.
source: Theophrastus, Characters 24 (Jebb 1870: "The Arrogant Man")

gloss: giving way to fear, seeing danger everywhere and slipping away from it
gloss_modern: This means seeing danger at every turn and running from it, letting fear decide what one does.
reasoning: This is giving way to fear, seeing danger everywhere and fleeing from it. Today it describes a person who lacks courage and shrinks from any risk.
source: Theophrastus, Characters 25 (Jebb 1870: "The Coward")

gloss: love of authority, greedy for power and gain, scorning the common people
gloss_modern: This means craving control and profit while looking down on ordinary people and treating them as beneath consideration.
reasoning: This is a love of authority combined with greed for power and gain, and contempt for the common people. Today it describes a person who craves control and advantage and looks down on ordinary people.
source: Theophrastus, Characters 26 (Jebb 1870: "The Oligarch")

gloss: taking up in old age the pursuits of youth, and making a fool of oneself
gloss_modern: This means taking up youthful pursuits late in life and embarrassing oneself by acting as if one were still young.
reasoning: This is taking up in old age the pursuits of youth and making a fool of oneself. Today it describes an older person who clings to youthful fashions and interests in an embarrassing way.
source: Theophrastus, Characters 27 (Jebb 1870: "The Late-Learner")

gloss: a habit of saying malicious and damaging things about others
gloss_modern: This means habitually saying spiteful, damaging things about absent people, leaving their reputations harmed.
reasoning: This is a habit of saying malicious and damaging things about others behind their backs. Today it is the habit of backbiting, spreading harmful talk about absent people.
source: Theophrastus, Characters 28 (Jebb 1870: "The Evil-Speaker")

gloss: a fondness for bad people, consorting with and defending rogues
gloss_modern: This means choosing to associate with dishonest people and standing up for rogues even when their conduct is plainly wrong.
reasoning: This is a fondness for bad people, consorting with them and defending rogues. Today it describes a person who keeps company with dishonest people and speaks up for them.
source: Theophrastus, Characters 29 (Jebb 1870: "The Patron of Rascals")

gloss: eagerness for base gain, profiting shabbily at the expense of others
gloss_modern: This means grasping eagerly for money and profiting shabbily at other people's expense, with no scruple about how.
reasoning: This is eagerness for base gain, profiting in a shabby way at others' expense. Today it describes a person who grasps for money by any means and takes advantage of others.
source: Theophrastus, Characters 30 (Jebb 1870: "The Avaricious Man")

gloss: an inflated sense of one's own worth, putting oneself above others
gloss_modern: This means thinking far more highly of oneself than of others and placing oneself above them.
reasoning: Pride is an inflated sense of one's own worth that places oneself above others. Today a person given to it is conceited and thinks themselves superior to everyone else.
source: the seven deadly sins (Gregory I's list, as later tradition names it)

gloss: a modest estimate of one's own importance, putting oneself no higher than others
gloss_modern: This means judging oneself realistically and placing oneself no higher than others, without boasting or self-importance.
reasoning: Humility is a modest estimate of one's own importance, placing oneself no higher than others. Today it is a person who is modest and unassuming about their worth.
source: the seven contrary virtues (after Prudentius, Psychomachia)

gloss: an insatiable desire for wealth and possessions
gloss_modern: This means always wanting more wealth and possessions, and never feeling satisfied with what one already has.
reasoning: Greed is an insatiable desire for wealth and possessions. Today it describes a person who always wants more money and goods and is never satisfied.
source: the seven deadly sins (Gregory I's list, as later tradition names it)

gloss: free and willing giving; charity toward those in need
gloss_modern: This means giving freely and willingly, especially to those in need, without holding back or keeping accounts.
reasoning: Liberality is free and willing giving, especially to those in need. Today it describes a person who gives generously and readily to others.
source: the seven contrary virtues (after Prudentius, Psychomachia)

gloss: an intense, uncontrolled desire for sexual pleasure
gloss_modern: This means being driven by an intense, uncontrolled craving for sexual gratification that overrides restraint.
reasoning: Lust is an intense, uncontrolled desire for sexual pleasure. Today it describes a person whose sexual appetite runs unchecked by restraint.
source: the seven deadly sins (Gregory I's list, as later tradition names it)

gloss: restraint and purity in sexual conduct
gloss_modern: This means keeping one's sexual conduct restrained and pure, controlling desire rather than indulging it.
reasoning: Chastity is restraint and purity in sexual conduct. Today it describes a person who is sexually restrained and faithful to their standards.
source: the seven contrary virtues (after Prudentius, Psychomachia)

gloss: resentment of others' goods, success or qualities, wishing them for oneself
gloss_modern: This means resenting others' success, goods or qualities and wishing they were one's own instead.
reasoning: Envy is resentment of others' goods, success or qualities, along with a wish to have them oneself. Today it describes a person who begrudges others their advantages.
source: the seven deadly sins (Gregory I's list, as later tradition names it)

gloss: good will toward others, rejoicing in their good
gloss_modern: This means wishing others well and feeling genuine gladness when they succeed or flourish.
reasoning: Kindness here is good will toward others, rejoicing in their good. Today it describes a person who is warm and benevolent and glad when others prosper.
source: the seven contrary virtues (after Prudentius, Psychomachia)

gloss: overindulgence in food and drink
gloss_modern: This means eating and drinking far beyond what is good for you, indulging appetite without any restraint.
reasoning: Gluttony is the sin of overindulging in food and drink, eating and drinking past what is good. Today's word for the person given to it is a glutton, or simply an overeater.
source: the seven deadly sins (Gregory I's list, as later tradition names it)

gloss: moderation in food and drink
gloss_modern: This means keeping your appetites for food and drink within sensible limits, enjoying them without excess.
reasoning: As the virtue opposed to gluttony, temperance is moderation in food and drink. The person who has it is temperate, keeping appetites within sensible limits.
source: the seven contrary virtues (after Prudentius, Psychomachia)

gloss: uncontrolled anger, hatred and the wish for revenge
gloss_modern: This means nursing uncontrolled anger and hatred, and burning to take revenge on those who wronged you.
reasoning: Wrath is uncontrolled anger joined with hatred and a wish for revenge. The person given to it is wrathful, or vengeful when the desire for payback dominates.
source: the seven deadly sins (Gregory I's list, as later tradition names it)

gloss: bearing provocation and delay calmly, without resentment
gloss_modern: This means enduring provocation and delay calmly, without holding grudges or resentment toward those who cause it.
reasoning: Patience is bearing provocation and delay calmly and without resentment, the opposite of wrath. The person who has it is patient, or forbearing toward those who try them.
source: the seven contrary virtues (after Prudentius, Psychomachia)

gloss: laziness and indifference about one's duties and the good
gloss_modern: This means avoiding effort and duty, and feeling indifferent about your obligations and about what is good.
reasoning: Sloth here is laziness and indifference toward one's duties and toward the good. The person given to it is slothful, or lazy in the ordinary sense of avoiding effort.
source: the seven deadly sins (Gregory I's list, as later tradition names it)

gloss: careful, steady effort in one's work and duties
gloss_modern: This means working steadily and carefully at your tasks and duties, sustaining effort without needing much prodding.
reasoning: Diligence is careful, steady effort in work and duties, the opposite of sloth. The person who has it is diligent, working faithfully without needing prodding.
source: the seven contrary virtues (after Prudentius, Psychomachia)

gloss: the practical wisdom to judge what is right to do in the circumstances
gloss_modern: This means weighing the circumstances wisely and judging what is right to do, acting sensibly rather than rashly.
reasoning: Prudence is practical wisdom, the ability to judge what is right to do in particular circumstances. The person who has it is prudent, acting sensibly rather than rashly.
source: the four cardinal virtues (Plato, Republic IV; Ambrose)

gloss: giving each person their due, in word and deed
gloss_modern: This means giving everyone their due, and treating others fairly in both what you say and what you do.
reasoning: Justice is giving each person their due in word and deed. The person who has it is just, or fair-minded in dealings with others.
source: the four cardinal virtues (Plato, Republic IV; Ambrose)

gloss: courage and endurance in the face of danger, pain and hardship
gloss_modern: This means facing danger, pain and hardship steadily, and enduring them rather than fleeing or giving way.
reasoning: Fortitude is courage and endurance in the face of danger, pain and hardship. The person who has it is courageous, standing firm rather than fleeing or giving way.
source: the four cardinal virtues (Plato, Republic IV; Ambrose)

gloss: self-restraint and moderation in every pleasure
gloss_modern: This means holding back from every pleasure in measure, keeping your desires in check across all areas of life.
reasoning: As a cardinal virtue, temperance is self-restraint and moderation in every pleasure. The person who has it is self-restrained, keeping desires in check in all areas of life.
source: the four cardinal virtues (Plato, Republic IV; Ambrose)

gloss: firm belief in God and in what has been revealed
gloss_modern: This means holding firm belief in God and in what has been revealed, and living by that faith.
reasoning: Faith is firm belief in God and in what has been revealed. The person who has it is devout, living by that belief.
source: the three theological virtues (1 Corinthians 13)

gloss: confident expectation of the good to come, and trust in its promise
gloss_modern: This means confidently expecting good to come and trusting its promise, even when present circumstances look bleak.
reasoning: Hope is confident expectation of the good to come, trusting its promise. The person who has it is hopeful, or optimistic about what lies ahead.
source: the three theological virtues (1 Corinthians 13)

gloss: love of God and of one's neighbor, shown in self-giving
gloss_modern: This means loving God and your neighbor, and giving of yourself generously to help others.
reasoning: Charity here is love of God and neighbor shown through self-giving. The person who has it is charitable, generous in helping others.
source: the three theological virtues (1 Corinthians 13)

gloss: thinking of new and productive ways to do things
gloss_modern: This means thinking up new and productive ways of doing things, and bringing fresh ideas to problems.
reasoning: Creativity is thinking of new and productive ways to do things. The person who has it is creative, and inventive in finding fresh solutions.

gloss: creativity used too little, or not at all, where it would serve
gloss_modern: This means rarely bringing fresh ideas to bear, even where new approaches would help, and sticking to routine.
reasoning: Conformity is the underuse of creativity, where new approaches would serve but are not tried. The person who has it is unimaginative, sticking to the conventional way.

gloss: creativity used too much, past the point where it serves
gloss_modern: This means pursuing novel and odd schemes past the point where they help, leaving others struggling to follow you.
reasoning: Eccentricity is creativity used past the point where it serves, producing odd schemes that others cannot follow. The person who has it is eccentric, or unconventional to a fault.

gloss: taking an interest in experience for its own sake, exploring and discovering
gloss_modern: This means wanting to experience and understand things for their own sake, exploring and discovering eagerly.
reasoning: Curiosity is interest in experience for its own sake, exploring and discovering. The person who has it is curious, or inquisitive about how things work.
source: Niemiec (2019), 'Finding the golden mean: the overuse, underuse, and optimal use of character strengths', Counselling Psychology Quarterly 32(3-4), 453-471, doi:10.1080/09515070.2019.1617674, Table 1 (paywalled, not read at verification); the labels are the noun nomenclature of Freidlin, Littman-Ovadia & Niemiec (2017), 'Positive psychopathology: social anxiety via character strengths underuse and overuse', Personality and Individual Differences 108, 50-54, Table 1 (which credits it to Niemiec 2014)

gloss: curiosity used too little, or not at all, where it would serve
gloss_modern: This means showing little interest in learning or experience, leaving things unexplored even where exploring would serve.
reasoning: Disinterest is the underuse of curiosity, where exploring would serve but is not done. The person who has it is incurious, showing little interest in learning or experience.

gloss: curiosity used too much, past the point where it serves
gloss_modern: This means poking into others' private affairs and asking too many questions, past what is needed or welcome.
reasoning: Nosiness is curiosity used too much, prying into matters that are none of one's business. The person who has it is nosy, or prying into others' affairs.

gloss: thinking things through and examining them from all sides; not jumping to conclusions
gloss_modern: This means thinking matters through and examining them from every side, refusing to jump to hasty conclusions.
reasoning: Judgment is thinking things through and examining them from all sides without jumping to conclusions. The person who has it is discerning, and open-minded to evidence.
source: Niemiec (2019), 'Finding the golden mean: the overuse, underuse, and optimal use of character strengths', Counselling Psychology Quarterly 32(3-4), 453-471, doi:10.1080/09515070.2019.1617674, Table 1 (paywalled, not read at verification); the labels are the noun nomenclature of Freidlin, Littman-Ovadia & Niemiec (2017), 'Positive psychopathology: social anxiety via character strengths underuse and overuse', Personality and Individual Differences 108, 50-54, Table 1 (which credits it to Niemiec 2014)

gloss: judgment used too little, or not at all, where it would serve
gloss_modern: This means they act on first impressions and rarely weigh evidence or consequences before deciding what to do.
reasoning: Judgment is the strength of thinking things through, and its underuse names someone who acts on impulse or first impressions without weighing evidence or consequences. Today that person is simply someone who does not stop to reflect before deciding.
source: Niemiec (2019), 'Finding the golden mean: the overuse, underuse, and optimal use of character strengths', Counselling Psychology Quarterly 32(3-4), 453-471, doi:10.1080/09515070.2019.1617674, Table 1 (paywalled, not read at verification); the labels are the noun nomenclature of Freidlin, Littman-Ovadia & Niemiec (2017), 'Positive psychopathology: social anxiety via character strengths underuse and overuse', Personality and Individual Differences 108, 50-54, Table 1 (which credits it to Niemiec 2014)

gloss: judgment used too much, past the point where it serves
gloss_modern: This means they assume bad motives behind everything people do and dismiss sincere efforts as naive or self-serving.
reasoning: Judgment in excess becomes a habit of doubting every motive and dismissing every claim as self-interest. The person who has it today is a cynic who distrusts others and sees the worst in everything.
source: Niemiec (2019), 'Finding the golden mean: the overuse, underuse, and optimal use of character strengths', Counselling Psychology Quarterly 32(3-4), 453-471, doi:10.1080/09515070.2019.1617674, Table 1 (paywalled, not read at verification); the labels are the noun nomenclature of Freidlin, Littman-Ovadia & Niemiec (2017), 'Positive psychopathology: social anxiety via character strengths underuse and overuse', Personality and Individual Differences 108, 50-54, Table 1 (which credits it to Niemiec 2014)

gloss: mastering new skills, topics and bodies of knowledge
gloss_modern: This means they seek out new skills and subjects with enthusiasm, studying steadily and enjoying the work of mastering them.
reasoning: This strength is a delight in mastering new skills, topics and bodies of knowledge. The person who has it is a lifelong learner who studies eagerly and seeks out new understanding.
source: Niemiec (2019), 'Finding the golden mean: the overuse, underuse, and optimal use of character strengths', Counselling Psychology Quarterly 32(3-4), 453-471, doi:10.1080/09515070.2019.1617674, Table 1 (paywalled, not read at verification); the labels are the noun nomenclature of Freidlin, Littman-Ovadia & Niemiec (2017), 'Positive psychopathology: social anxiety via character strengths underuse and overuse', Personality and Individual Differences 108, 50-54, Table 1 (which credits it to Niemiec 2014)

gloss: love of learning used too little, or not at all, where it would serve
gloss_modern: This means they feel satisfied with what they already know and never bother to learn anything new.
reasoning: Complacency is the underuse of the love of learning, a contentment with what one already knows. The person who has it today is self-satisfied and incurious, making no effort to learn anything new.
source: Niemiec (2019), 'Finding the golden mean: the overuse, underuse, and optimal use of character strengths', Counselling Psychology Quarterly 32(3-4), 453-471, doi:10.1080/09515070.2019.1617674, Table 1 (paywalled, not read at verification); the labels are the noun nomenclature of Freidlin, Littman-Ovadia & Niemiec (2017), 'Positive psychopathology: social anxiety via character strengths underuse and overuse', Personality and Individual Differences 108, 50-54, Table 1 (which credits it to Niemiec 2014)

gloss: love of learning used too much, past the point where it serves
gloss_modern: This means they flaunt their learning, correcting trivial points and lecturing others rather than sharing knowledge helpfully.
reasoning: Too much love of learning turns into displaying one's learning, lecturing and correcting others on minor points. The person today is a pedant who shows off knowledge rather than sharing it.

gloss: being able to give wise counsel; seeing the world in ways that make sense to oneself and others
gloss_modern: This means they see situations clearly and offer sound advice that helps others make sense of what is happening.
reasoning: Perspective is the ability to give wise counsel and see the world in ways that make sense to oneself and others. The person who has it is a sound adviser who sees situations clearly and helps others understand them.
source: Niemiec (2019), 'Finding the golden mean: the overuse, underuse, and optimal use of character strengths', Counselling Psychology Quarterly 32(3-4), 453-471, doi:10.1080/09515070.2019.1617674, Table 1 (paywalled, not read at verification); the labels are the noun nomenclature of Freidlin, Littman-Ovadia & Niemiec (2017), 'Positive psychopathology: social anxiety via character strengths underuse and overuse', Personality and Individual Differences 108, 50-54, Table 1 (which credits it to Niemiec 2014)

gloss: perspective used too little, or not at all, where it would serve
gloss_modern: This means they grasp only the surface of situations and offer thin, unhelpful views instead of real insight.
reasoning: Shallowness is the underuse of perspective, grasping only surface features and offering thin views. The person who has it today is superficial, lacking depth of understanding.
source: Niemiec (2019), 'Finding the golden mean: the overuse, underuse, and optimal use of character strengths', Counselling Psychology Quarterly 32(3-4), 453-471, doi:10.1080/09515070.2019.1617674, Table 1 (paywalled, not read at verification); the labels are the noun nomenclature of Freidlin, Littman-Ovadia & Niemiec (2017), 'Positive psychopathology: social anxiety via character strengths underuse and overuse', Personality and Individual Differences 108, 50-54, Table 1 (which credits it to Niemiec 2014)

gloss: perspective used too much, past the point where it serves
gloss_modern: This means they press their views and advice on others so forcefully that people feel overruled and stop listening.
reasoning: Too much perspective becomes pressing one's views and advice on others until they feel overruled. The person today is domineering, forcing their outlook on people who stop listening.

gloss: not shrinking from threat, challenge, difficulty or pain; speaking up for what is right
gloss_modern: This means they face danger, difficulty or pain steadily and speak up for what is right despite the risk.
reasoning: Bravery is not shrinking from threat, difficulty or pain and speaking up for what is right. The person who has it is courageous, facing danger and standing up for principle.
source: Niemiec (2019), 'Finding the golden mean: the overuse, underuse, and optimal use of character strengths', Counselling Psychology Quarterly 32(3-4), 453-471, doi:10.1080/09515070.2019.1617674, Table 1 (paywalled, not read at verification); the labels are the noun nomenclature of Freidlin, Littman-Ovadia & Niemiec (2017), 'Positive psychopathology: social anxiety via character strengths underuse and overuse', Personality and Individual Differences 108, 50-54, Table 1 (which credits it to Niemiec 2014)

gloss: bravery used too little, or not at all, where it would serve
gloss_modern: This means they shrink from threats, challenges or pain, and avoid speaking up even when they should.
reasoning: Cowardice is the underuse of bravery, shrinking from threat or challenge where courage is needed. The person who has it today is timid and fearful, avoiding what they should face.
source: Niemiec (2019), 'Finding the golden mean: the overuse, underuse, and optimal use of character strengths', Counselling Psychology Quarterly 32(3-4), 453-471, doi:10.1080/09515070.2019.1617674, Table 1 (paywalled, not read at verification); the labels are the noun nomenclature of Freidlin, Littman-Ovadia & Niemiec (2017), 'Positive psychopathology: social anxiety via character strengths underuse and overuse', Personality and Individual Differences 108, 50-54, Table 1 (which credits it to Niemiec 2014)

gloss: bravery used too much, past the point where it serves
gloss_modern: This means they take needless risks with danger, ignoring the consequences in a rash display of boldness.
reasoning: Foolhardiness is bravery in excess, boldness that ignores real danger. The person today is reckless, courting risk without regard for consequences.
source: Niemiec (2019), 'Finding the golden mean: the overuse, underuse, and optimal use of character strengths', Counselling Psychology Quarterly 32(3-4), 453-471, doi:10.1080/09515070.2019.1617674, Table 1 (paywalled, not read at verification); the labels are the noun nomenclature of Freidlin, Littman-Ovadia & Niemiec (2017), 'Positive psychopathology: social anxiety via character strengths underuse and overuse', Personality and Individual Differences 108, 50-54, Table 1 (which credits it to Niemiec 2014)

gloss: finishing what one starts; persisting in the face of obstacles
gloss_modern: This means they finish what they start and keep working toward their goals through obstacles and setbacks.
reasoning: Perseverance is finishing what one starts and persisting despite obstacles. The person who has it is steadfast and keeps working toward goals through setbacks.
source: Niemiec (2019), 'Finding the golden mean: the overuse, underuse, and optimal use of character strengths', Counselling Psychology Quarterly 32(3-4), 453-471, doi:10.1080/09515070.2019.1617674, Table 1 (paywalled, not read at verification); the labels are the noun nomenclature of Freidlin, Littman-Ovadia & Niemiec (2017), 'Positive psychopathology: social anxiety via character strengths underuse and overuse', Personality and Individual Differences 108, 50-54, Table 1 (which credits it to Niemiec 2014)

gloss: perseverance used too little, or not at all, where it would serve
gloss_modern: This means they abandon projects at the first obstacle or setback and fail to finish what they begin.
reasoning: Fragility is the underuse of perseverance, giving up when obstacles appear. The person who has it today is irresolute, abandoning efforts at the first difficulty.
source: Niemiec (2019), 'Finding the golden mean: the overuse, underuse, and optimal use of character strengths', Counselling Psychology Quarterly 32(3-4), 453-471, doi:10.1080/09515070.2019.1617674, Table 1 (paywalled, not read at verification); the labels are the noun nomenclature of Freidlin, Littman-Ovadia & Niemiec (2017), 'Positive psychopathology: social anxiety via character strengths underuse and overuse', Personality and Individual Differences 108, 50-54, Table 1 (which credits it to Niemiec 2014)

gloss: perseverance used too much, past the point where it serves
gloss_modern: This means they press on toward a goal past all sense, unable to let go even when it harms them or others.
reasoning: Obsessiveness is perseverance in excess, pressing on past all sense and being unable to let go. The person today is obsessive, fixated on a goal even when it harms them.

gloss: speaking the truth and presenting oneself genuinely
gloss_modern: This means they tell the truth and present themselves as they really are, without pretence or deception.
reasoning: Honesty is speaking the truth and presenting oneself genuinely. The person who has it is sincere, open about who they are and what they think.

gloss: honesty used too little, or not at all, where it would serve
gloss_modern: This means they pretend to be someone they are not, feign feelings, and mislead others about who they really are.
reasoning: Phoniness is the underuse of honesty, presenting a false self and feigning feelings. The person today is a fake, insincere in what they show others.

gloss: honesty used too much, past the point where it serves
gloss_modern: This means they blurt out harsh truths and moralize at others, smugly sure their candour is always a virtue.
reasoning: Righteousness here is honesty in excess, blurting out harsh truths and moralizing at others. The person today is self-righteous, smugly sure that their candour is always a virtue.

gloss: approaching life with excitement and energy
gloss_modern: This means they approach life with eagerness and vigor, throwing themselves into activities with real excitement.
reasoning: Zest is approaching life with excitement and energy. The person who has it is enthusiastic, throwing themselves into activities with real eagerness.
source: Niemiec (2019), 'Finding the golden mean: the overuse, underuse, and optimal use of character strengths', Counselling Psychology Quarterly 32(3-4), 453-471, doi:10.1080/09515070.2019.1617674, Table 1 (paywalled, not read at verification); the labels are the noun nomenclature of Freidlin, Littman-Ovadia & Niemiec (2017), 'Positive psychopathology: social anxiety via character strengths underuse and overuse', Personality and Individual Differences 108, 50-54, Table 1 (which credits it to Niemiec 2014)

gloss: zest used too little, or not at all, where it would serve
gloss_modern: This means they lack energy and drive, going through life flat and unmotivated, rarely excited about anything.
reasoning: Sedentary is the underuse of zest, a lack of energy and drive, leaving life flat. The person who has it today is listless and apathetic, rarely excited by anything.
source: Niemiec (2019), 'Finding the golden mean: the overuse, underuse, and optimal use of character strengths', Counselling Psychology Quarterly 32(3-4), 453-471, doi:10.1080/09515070.2019.1617674, Table 1 (paywalled, not read at verification); the labels are the noun nomenclature of Freidlin, Littman-Ovadia & Niemiec (2017), 'Positive psychopathology: social anxiety via character strengths underuse and overuse', Personality and Individual Differences 108, 50-54, Table 1 (which credits it to Niemiec 2014)

gloss: zest used too much, past the point where it serves

gloss: expecting the best in the future and working to achieve it
gloss_modern: This means expecting good outcomes from the future and acting with energy to bring them about.
reasoning: Hope means expecting the best in the future and working to achieve it. A hopeful person today looks ahead with confidence and acts to bring good outcomes about.

gloss: hope used too little, or not at all, where it would serve
gloss_modern: This means expecting the worst, doubting that things will improve, and failing to act on chances for something better.

gloss: hope used too much, past the point where it serves
gloss_modern: This means insisting everything will turn out well and brushing aside real problems and dangers with cheerful denial.
reasoning: The item is Pollyanna-ism, hope so unshaken that it denies real problems and dangers. Today this is a naively optimistic person who waves away every difficulty.

gloss: liking to laugh and tease; bringing smiles to other people
gloss_modern: This means enjoying laughter and teasing, and bringing lightness and smiles to the people around you.
reasoning: Humor here means liking to laugh and tease and bringing smiles to others. A person with it today is playful and lightens the mood for the people around them.
source: Niemiec (2019), 'Finding the golden mean: the overuse, underuse, and optimal use of character strengths', Counselling Psychology Quarterly 32(3-4), 453-471, doi:10.1080/09515070.2019.1617674, Table 1 (paywalled, not read at verification); the labels are the noun nomenclature of Freidlin, Littman-Ovadia & Niemiec (2017), 'Positive psychopathology: social anxiety via character strengths underuse and overuse', Personality and Individual Differences 108, 50-54, Table 1 (which credits it to Niemiec 2014)

gloss: humor used too little, or not at all, where it would serve
gloss_modern: This means staying grave and stiff even where lightness would ease tension or help people connect.
reasoning: The VIA underuse name for humor is over-seriousness, meaning a person who withholds lightness even where it would ease tension or help. Today that person is plainly humorless and stiff.

gloss: humor used too much, past the point where it serves
gloss_modern: This means turning nearly everything into a joke and clowning around, even when the moment calls for seriousness.
reasoning: Giddiness names humor used past the point where it serves, so the person jokes and clowns constantly, even when seriousness is needed. Today we call that person buffoonish or flippant.
source: Niemiec (2019), 'Finding the golden mean: the overuse, underuse, and optimal use of character strengths', Counselling Psychology Quarterly 32(3-4), 453-471, doi:10.1080/09515070.2019.1617674, Table 1 (paywalled, not read at verification); the labels are the noun nomenclature of Freidlin, Littman-Ovadia & Niemiec (2017), 'Positive psychopathology: social anxiety via character strengths underuse and overuse', Personality and Individual Differences 108, 50-54, Table 1 (which credits it to Niemiec 2014)

gloss: having coherent beliefs about the higher purpose and meaning of life
gloss_modern: This means holding a steady sense of life's larger meaning and purpose, and living by it day to day.
reasoning: This strength is holding coherent beliefs about the higher purpose and meaning of life, so the person has a settled sense of what matters and why. Today that person is called spiritual.
source: Niemiec (2019), 'Finding the golden mean: the overuse, underuse, and optimal use of character strengths', Counselling Psychology Quarterly 32(3-4), 453-471, doi:10.1080/09515070.2019.1617674, Table 1 (paywalled, not read at verification); the labels are the noun nomenclature of Freidlin, Littman-Ovadia & Niemiec (2017), 'Positive psychopathology: social anxiety via character strengths underuse and overuse', Personality and Individual Differences 108, 50-54, Table 1 (which credits it to Niemiec 2014)

gloss: spirituality used too little, or not at all, where it would serve
gloss_modern: This means lacking any settled view of life's purpose, so one drifts without a sense of why things matter.
reasoning: Anomie, the underuse of spirituality, means lacking any coherent view of life's purpose, so one drifts with no sense of why things matter. Today that person is spiritually adrift and rootless.
source: Niemiec (2019), 'Finding the golden mean: the overuse, underuse, and optimal use of character strengths', Counselling Psychology Quarterly 32(3-4), 453-471, doi:10.1080/09515070.2019.1617674, Table 1 (paywalled, not read at verification); the labels are the noun nomenclature of Freidlin, Littman-Ovadia & Niemiec (2017), 'Positive psychopathology: social anxiety via character strengths underuse and overuse', Personality and Individual Differences 108, 50-54, Table 1 (which credits it to Niemiec 2014)

gloss: spirituality used too much, past the point where it serves
gloss_modern: This means pressing one's beliefs about ultimate meaning with rigid zeal, allowing no doubt, and treating disagreement as enemy.
reasoning: Fanaticism is spirituality used past the point of serving, so the person holds beliefs about ultimate meaning with rigid zeal and no room for doubt. Today we call that person fanatical.
